name: Long gamma scalping
heading: The Structural Opportunity: Profiting from Realised Volatility
caseLead: Long gamma scalping can generate returns when realised price moves are large enough to cover the cost of options and repeated hedging. The opportunity persists because insurers, structured product issuers and yield-seeking funds supply options at prices based on average conditions, while geopolitical and policy events produce bursts of movement that those averages understate.
caseRest: The strategy loses option premium to time decay when realised volatility is too low to cover the cost of the position and its hedges. Each hedge also costs a small amount in spreads and slippage, so a long period of calm can produce losses over many months. Rehyn estimates that a prolonged low-volatility period, such as 2017, is the most damaging condition because gains from hedging arrive only when moves are large.
figNote: Each card shows the highest closing level of the VIX during the episode. The VIX measures the volatility that S&P 500 options price in for the next 30 days: it has averaged about 19 over the long run, while readings above 30 signal market stress.

events.title: US credit downgrade drives large daily moves
events.text: Standard and Poor's downgraded the US credit rating on 5 August 2011, and the VIX closed at 48 on 8 August. The strategy gained because the S&P 500 fell about 6.7% that day and further large daily moves followed.

events.title: UK vote to leave the European Union
events.text: The UK vote of 23 June 2016 to leave the European Union lifted the VIX to a 26 close as the S&P 500 fell about 3.6%. Results were mixed because the market recovered within days, so time decay offset part of the hedging gain.

events.title: North Korea tensions fail to sustain volatility
events.text: Threats between the US and North Korea lifted the VIX to a 16 close on 10 August 2017, when the S&P 500 fell about 1.5%. The strategy lost because the market recovered within days and realised volatility stayed below the level priced into options.

events.title: Covid turns into a global funding crisis
events.text: The March 2020 sell-off turned a health emergency into a global rush for cash, lifting the VIX to an 83 close on 16 March. The strategy gained because the S&P 500 fell about 12% that day and moves above 5% recurred through the month.

events.title: Bank of Japan rate rise unwinds yen trades
events.text: A Bank of Japan rate rise and weak US jobs data forced yen-funded trades to close, and the VIX closed at 39 on 5 August. Results were mixed because the S&P 500 recovered within two weeks, so time decay offset part of the gain.

events.title: US tariffs drive the largest spike since 2020
events.text: US tariff announcements lifted the VIX to a 52 close on 8 April 2025, after the S&P 500 fell about 6% on 4 April and rose about 9.5% on 9 April. The strategy gained because the options paid for large moves in both directions.

instrument: S&P 500 index options and E-mini S&P 500 futures; about 30 days to expiry; hedged intraday and rolled monthly
rules: At-the-money straddles bought when implied volatility is below forecast realised volatility; delta hedged with futures at each 0.25% move in the index; options closed before expiry
costs: Estimated option spreads, futures commissions and slippage on each hedge deducted
constructionTitle: Strategy construction, from realised volatility to hedge discipline

legs.position: Long straddle, 30 days, at the money
legs.purpose: Owns the moves that the hedging trades convert into gains
Offsets part of the premium cost
Removes market direction so gains come from movement
Provides collateral and earns the cash rate

entry: Implied volatility at least 1 point below the forecast of realised volatility
size: Premium capped at 4% of capital, scaled to a 7% annualised volatility target
exit: Options closed 10 days before expiry, or when time decay exceeds hedging gains
stop: All positions closed if losses reach 2% of capital in a month
marketWatch: The gap between implied volatility and recent daily index moves is the main indicator for this strategy, because it shows whether options are cheap compared with the market's movement. Scheduled central bank decisions, trade announcements and geopolitical deadlines matter because they can produce large daily moves in either direction. Rehyn also watches bid-ask spreads on index options, since wider spreads raise hedging costs.

favourable.heading: Clusters of large daily moves
favourable.text: Clusters of large daily moves favour the strategy because each hedge locks in a gain as the index swings back and forth. In March 2020 the S&P 500 moved by more than 5% on several days, far above the moves priced into options earlier in the year.

favourable.heading: Policy surprises that reprice risk
favourable.text: Unexpected policy decisions favour the strategy because they produce abrupt moves that option prices did not anticipate. The April 2025 tariff announcement was followed by a fall of about 6% in one day and a rise of about 9.5% in another.

favourable.heading: Cheap options before a turning point
favourable.text: Low implied volatility favours the strategy because options then cost little compared with the moves that follow. In February 2018 the VIX had closed near 11 in late January, and the index then fell about 4% on 5 February.

adverse.heading: Prolonged calm in index markets
adverse.text: Long periods of low realised volatility hurt the strategy because the premium paid decays each day while hedging produces little gain. The largest one-day fall in the S&P 500 in 2017 was about 1.8%, so options cost more than the hedging trades returned.

adverse.heading: Spikes that reverse within days
adverse.text: Sharp spikes that reverse quickly hurt the strategy because gains from the first large move are given back when the market recovers and the options lose value. After the Brexit vote in June 2016, the S&P 500 recovered its losses within about three weeks.

adverse.heading: Wider spreads in disorderly markets
adverse.text: Wider spreads in disorderly markets hurt the strategy because each hedge costs more and prices can gap between trades. Rehyn estimates that transaction costs rose several times in March 2020, which reduced the gain from a very large move.

infoHist: Historical results show the strategy's estimated return during each event, using index options held through the event and hedged at each 0.25% move in the index. Each event window runs from the last market high before the shock to the market low, with option decay and hedging costs included.
infoForward: Scenario results show the estimated profit or loss over the first month of each scenario. Rehyn's scenario engine projects the path of the S&P 500 and implied volatility, which are then applied to the strategy's options, with the hedging rules applied to the projected daily moves.
altTitle: Where Else Can Investors Find Long Volatility Returns?

related.why: Sells the index options this strategy buys. Bears crash risk, losing when volatility rises sharply.
Buys single-stock options before results. Bears premium decay, losing when announcements move shares less than priced.
Holds VIX futures for protection. Bears roll cost, paying steadily in calm markets and gaining in sell-offs.
